articles.title: Everything we know about Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua: Ring-walk times, undercard, press conference, world title
articles.summary: It has taken almost a decade to get to this point, so let's break it all down.
articles.body:
The biggest fight in British boxing history was made official Thursday morning when it was announced that heavyweights Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury would finally share a ring later this year.

It has taken almost a decade to get to this point. Fury and Joshua held heavyweight world titles as early as 2016, but a clash ultimately never materialized. Talks reignited on separate occasions in 2019, 2021 and 2022 — with the pair even owning all four championships between them in 2021 — yet were unsuccessful every time.

In 2026, Fury, 38, and Joshua, 36, are in the final stretches of their storied careers, and now they'll finally deliver the fight boxing fans have been waiting for.

Fury and Joshua collide on Dec. 11 at Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales.

The Welsh venue can accommodate around 80,000 spectators — 15,000 fewer than the national stadium, Wembley Stadium; however, Principality has a fully retractable roof, making it a better fit for an outdoor event in December.

When will Fury and Joshua make their ring walks?

Although ring-walk times are currently unofficial, it is expected Fury and Joshua will enter the ring in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK to cater to a primetime U.S. audience on Friday night.

The first bell will likely ring between 9-10 p.m. ET on Netflix.

Joshua and Fury will have the chance to become three-time heavyweight champions on Dec. 11 with the vacant WBA (Super) heavyweight title on the line.

Other heavyweight titleholders include Filip Hrgovic (IBF), Daniel Dubois (WBO) and Agit Kabayel (WBC). Murat Gassiev is the secondary WBA heavyweight champion.

Fury and Joshua will come face-to-face for the first time since their bout was announced at a press conference Sept. 30 at British Airways Arc in London.

UFC CEO Dana White has long claimed that he will promote the showdown between the British heavyweight giants. Joshua's promoter, Eddie Hearn, and Fury's promoter, Frank Warren, however, have both said that White, his promotion Zuffa Boxing, and TKO — the parent company of the UFC — are barred from promotional involvement in the event.

In the fight announcement, Netflix stated that Turki Alalshikh's "The Ring" and White would collaborate to promote Fury vs. Joshua. Hearn has since reiterated publicly that this would not be the case.

The undercard has not been announced yet, but several fights are in contention.

It has been reported in recent days — and Uncrowned can confirm — that talks are ongoing to place four-division champion Shakur Stevenson in the co-feature slot against the legendary Manny Pacquiao.

Another fight that is likely to take place on the bill is an all-American welterweight showdown between Keyshawn Davis and Richardson Hitchins.

Newly crowned IBF heavyweight champion Filip Hrgovic could land a slot on the bill against Rico Verhoeven or Frank Sanchez.

articles.title: Johnny Fisher vs Michael Pirotton:  Free live stream of final press conference ahead of Copper Box heavyweight clash
articles.summary: Johnny Fisher returns to heavyweight action at the Copper Box against Belgium's determined Michael Pirotton, with Craig Richards vs Radivoje Kalajdzic, Lee Cutler vs Louis Greene and much more on the card; Watch Zuffa Boxing 11 on Saturday live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Johnny Fisher's heavyweight clash with Michael Pirotton in London on Saturday will be live on Sky Sports .

First they face one another at the final press conference at the Copper Box Arena from 6pm.

Heavyweight hitter Johnny Fisher is looking to kickstart a surge up the ranks, while Belgium's Pirotton is determined to make a name for himself against the hugely popular "Romford Bull".

Their fight headlines Zuffa Boxing 11 at the Copper Box that sees a raft of 50-50 fights and unbeatens matched against one another.

Zuffa Boxing 11 also features former world light-heavyweight title challenger Craig Richards against Radivoje "Hot Rod" Kalajdzic in the chief support.

British middleweights Lee Cutler and Louis Greene will go to war in an all-action bout.

Cesar Mateo Tapia , unbeaten in 19 pro contests, takes on Leo Ruiz , a Mexican based in California with a 17-1 record.

Kayla Allen will make her professional debut while Alex MacMillan will look to continue his winning run against 2-0 Frenchman Guillaume Azagier .

London-based Moldovan Aurel Ignat , who shocked Scott Forrest with a first-round KO win last year, will put his unbeaten record on the line against Mexican Olympian Rogelio Romero , a 6-0 prospect from Juarez who has a 100 per cent knockout ratio.

Fred Pullen , a national champion as an amateur, makes his pro debut against Italy's Leonardo Faretina and in a clash of unbeaten prospects, America's Alexis De La Cerda meets Ireland's Cain Lewis .

articles.title: Inspiring story of brotherhood: “Our relationship is much, much different. We have a brotherhood.”-  How Khabib Nurmagomedov and Islam Makhachev built a bond that goes far beyond MMA
articles.summary: Khabib Nurmagomedov and Islam Makhachev have spent so much of their lives together that calling them simply teammates or training partners does not really
articles.body: Khabib Nurmagomedov and Islam Makhachev have spent so much of their lives together that calling them simply teammates or training partners does not really explain their relationship. The two fighters grew up around the same people, went to school together, trained under Khabib’s father Abdulmanap Nurmagomedov and eventually reached the highest level of mixed martial arts together. That long history is why Khabib has always spoken about Makhachev in a very personal way, and one quote from the former UFC champion explains it better than almost anything else. “Our relationship is much, much different. We have a brotherhood,” Khabib said, making it clear that his connection with Makhachev was built long before the UFC, championships or worldwide fame became part of their lives.What did Khabib mean when he called his relationship with Makhachev a brotherhood?When Khabib called his relationship with Makhachev a brotherhood, he was explaining that their connection cannot be understood only through their work in MMA. The two men did not meet after becoming professional fighters and decide to train together. Their relationship goes back to childhood, when neither of them could have known how far their careers would eventually take them.Khabib has explained that they knew each other for around 25 years, grew up together and went to school together. They also had the same coach and shared many experiences while growing up in Dagestan. Those memories created a relationship that was already strong before either fighter became a major name in the sport.That is an important part of understanding Khabib’s quote. When he says they have a brotherhood, he is not simply using the word to describe how close teammates can become after years of training. He is talking about a relationship that was formed during their childhood and continued through every major stage of their lives.Their journey also brought them into the same training environment under Abdulmanap, who became one of the most important figures in both men’s lives. They learned the same lessons, followed the same training methods and spent years pushing each other during practice. The sport became one part of a relationship that had already existed for years.For Khabib, therefore, Makhachev is not just someone who shares his professional ambitions. He is someone who has been part of his life for a very long time.Why does Khabib see Islam Makhachev as more than a training partner?Khabib has repeatedly made it clear that the word “training partner” does not go far enough when describing Makhachev. Their time together inside the gym is only one part of a much larger story that includes school, family, friendship and the influence of Abdulmanap.Khabib once explained that he feels especially happy when his teammates and close friends win, saying, “I am happy with my guys, my brothers, when they win, more than when I win.” That statement helps explain why he became such an important figure during Makhachev’s rise through the UFC.For many fighters, a training partner is someone who helps prepare them for a particular fight. The relationship can be built around technique, fitness and competition, but Khabib’s connection with Makhachev is different because it existed long before the two had professional careers to support.Khabib has also spent years encouraging Makhachev and believing in his ability to become a champion. Even before Makhachev reached the top of the UFC lightweight division, Khabib regularly spoke about his potential and the qualities that made him different from other fighters.Their relationship also became more visible as Makhachev’s career grew. Khabib was often around him during major fights, helped him prepare and stood beside him during some of the biggest moments of his career. When Makhachev defeated Charles Oliveira at UFC 280 in 2022 to win the UFC lightweight championship, Khabib was there to celebrate the achievement.For Khabib, watching Makhachev reach that point was not simply another fighter winning a title. It was someone he had known since childhood reaching a goal they had worked toward for years.How did Abdulmanap Nurmagomedov bring Khabib and Makhachev even closer?Abdulmanap Nurmagomedov is an important part of the story because he was much more than a coach to both Khabib and Makhachev. He helped shape the way they trained, competed and understood discipline, while also creating the environment in which their relationship became even stronger.Khabib’s own career was built around the lessons he learned from his father, and Makhachev became another important student within that system. Both fighters developed their wrestling and grappling skills under Abdulmanap and became part of the same close training group.That shared connection became even more meaningful after Abdulmanap died in 2020. Khabib had already retired from professional MMA by then, but his relationship with Makhachev continued to grow. Helping Makhachev succeed became connected to the legacy that Abdulmanap had left behind.Makhachev has also spoken about Khabib as an older brother who helped show him the way. That description explains why the relationship continued even after Makhachev became a champion in his own right. Becoming a UFC champion changed Makhachev’s status in the sport, but it did not change the personal relationship between the two men.There is also a sense of responsibility in Khabib’s support for Makhachev. He has often spoken about wanting his teammates to achieve as much as possible, and his support for Makhachev has gone beyond simply giving fight advice. He has helped carry forward the training system and values that he learned from Abdulmanap.In that sense, Makhachev’s career represents another part of the story that Khabib and his father started building years ago.Why is Khabib and Makhachev’s relationship so important to both fighters?The simplest reason is that their relationship was never created by fame. It existed before the UFC, before championship belts and before millions of fans knew their names.Khabib and Makhachev grew up together and shared experiences that have nothing to do with MMA. They went to school together, trained together and became part of the same sporting family. That history gives their relationship a level of trust that cannot easily be created between two athletes who meet later in their careers.Makhachev has also made it clear that he values Khabib’s guidance. Even after becoming a UFC champion, he has continued to speak about Khabib with the respect normally given to an older brother or mentor. Their relationship has therefore developed beyond the traditional fighter and coach dynamic.Khabib’s quote, “Our relationship is much, much different. We have a brotherhood,” makes sense when that history is taken into account. He was not trying to describe a normal friendship between two fighters. He was explaining why Makhachev’s victories mean so much to him and why he has remained so closely involved in his career.Their story is ultimately about two athletes who grew up together and found their way into the same sport under the guidance of the same coach. One became a UFC champion and retired as one of the most respected fighters of his generation, while the other followed the same path and eventually reached the championship level himself.For Khabib, Makhachev’s success is therefore personal. He is watching someone he has known since childhood continue a journey they started together many years ago. That is what makes the word “brotherhood” more meaningful than simply calling them teammates. articles.title: Gaethje: "Ilia Topuria no volverá a ser campeón de peso ligero"
articles.standfirst: El peleador estadounidense cree que 'El Matador' es demasiado pequeño para la división, y ha afirmado que si no se retira le dará la oportunidad titular a Arman Tsarukyan
articles.summary: El peleador estadounidense cree que 'El Matador' es demasiado pequeño para la división, y ha afirmado que si no se retira le dará la oportunidad titular a Arman Tsarukyan
articles.body: Justin Gaethje ha dado nuevas pistas sobre su futuro y ha vuelto a atacar a Ilia Topuria tras una nueva aparición pública, donde ha afirmado que 'El Matador' no volverá a ser campeón de peso ligero. De hecho, el peleador estadounidense le ha recomendado bajar de nuevo a peso pluma, y ha revelado que en caso de que no se retire le dará la oportunidad por el cinturón a Arman Tsarukyan. El objetivo de Topuria es que Gaethje le conceda una revancha por el cinturón de peso ligero tras arrebatárselo en el UFC Casa Blanca, pero 'The Highlight' no parece muy por la labor. La semana pasada llegó a afirmar que estaría dispuesto a un nuevo combate entre ambos tras las provocaciones de Ilia, pero ha vuelto a cambiar su discurso y esta vez parece la definitiva. De hecho, en una entrevista con con Andrew Schulz en el podcast 'Flagrant' la ha recomendado bajar de nuevo a peso pluma, donde ya noqueó a Alexander Volkanovski y Max Holloway durante su reinado. "No creo que llegue a ser campeón de peso ligero. No puede vencer a Arman Tsarukyan y lo va a pasar mal con Paddy Pimblett. Hay un montón de tipos duros. Creo que es demasiado pequeño para el peso ligero. Esa es la impresión que me dio". Lo cierto es que en peso ligero Ilia se convirtió en campeón en junio de 2025 tras noquear en el primer asalto a Charles Oliveira, que sometió en su momento a Gaethje también en el primer asalto. Hace un año se decía que Ilia era demasiado pequeño para la división, pero no hay que olvidar que a Justin también estuvo a punto de noquearle en el segundo asalto con un golpe al cuerpo y fue su esquina la que tuvo que parar la pelea, ya que el estadounidense no logró el K.O. a pesar de lo mucho que lo intentó. Gaethje no quiere darle una oportunidad de redención a Topuria, y prueba de ello han sido sus palabras en ese mismo podcast en las que ha afirmado que "Arman es el siguiente en la lista. Si llego a defender este campeonato, será contra él con quien pelee. Simplemente no lo sé en este momento. Voy a disfrutar de ser el campeón durante el resto del año. Tomaré una decisión tanto de negocios como de vida cuando llegue el momento". Tsarukyan noqueó a Mauricio Ruffy este pasado sábado en el UFC 331, y él mismo reconoció que la compañía le ha asegurado una pelea por el cinturón. Eso sí, tendrá que esperar hasta 2027, e incluso cabe la posibilidad de que Gaethje se retire incluso antes de llegar a defender el cinturón una sola vez. "Todo el mundo dice: "Pelea contra Arman". Tengo lesiones que debo atender. No he tomado una decisión. Tengo 37 años. He tenido 40 peleas. No lo sé. No necesito volver a pelear", finalizó Justin. Por tanto, los próximos meses serán claves para conocer el futuro de una de las divisiones más talentosas y mediáticas de la UFC, que actualmente se encuentra al rojo vivo.

articles.title: Fury vs Joshua: The compromises & power struggles that shaped heavyweight fight
articles.summary: BBC Sport takes a look at the compromises, power struggles and competing interests behind Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua.
articles.body:
After a decade of stalled negotiations, public squabbling and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in the ring on 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium.

BBC Sport understands the WBA 'Super' heavyweight title is expected to be on the line, although confirmation from the governing body is still awaited.

It would give both former world champions the chance to regain a version of the heavyweight crown, although Fury-Joshua has always been about more than belts.

The fight arrives later than anybody wanted, with both in the twilight of their careers, but for years British boxing's biggest heavyweight rivalry seemed destined to remain a story of what might have been.

Yet Thursday's announcement of an 80,000-capacity showdown, broadcast globally by Netflix, did more than finally provide a date and venue.

It also offered a glimpse of the competing interests, egos and power struggles involved in getting one of boxing's most elusive fights over the line.

How compromise finally got the fight made

Speaking to BBC Sport after the fight was announced, Fury's promoter Frank Warren repeatedly returned to one word: compromise.

"Everybody's got to make a compromise," the Queensberry boss said. "Tyson really compromised. He didn't dig his heels in.

"He said, 'Fine, wherever they want it, I'll do it. If they want me to go to New York, I'll go. They want it in the UK, I just want to get the fight on."

The fighters had already agreed to the contest but the venue was a sticking point.

Warren says Netflix wanted New York, while Joshua, 36, was determined to fight in Britain. Predictably, their camps disagree over who finally got it done.

Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn described the push to keep the fight in Britain as a "two-man crusade".

"AJ has turned down money to keep it in the UK," Hearn told the Matchroom YouTube channel. "I wouldn't be able to look people in the eye if I was part of the movement to take this to the US."

Hearn says Joshua had specifically requested protection for a UK fight in his contract and refused to relent.

"We were under so much pressure to fold," he added. "It was only really the support of the British public that made Joshua stand 10 toes down and say no."

He says Fury, 38, could have insisted on his own contractual position but instead accepted Britain to ensure the fight did not collapse.

The power struggle and Dana White sideshow

Perhaps the biggest sideshow has been the struggle for influence around the promotion itself.

Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the fight, having previously insisted any confirmation would come from him.

"For 15 years no-one has been able to make this fight," he wrote. "Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury v Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over."

Dana White's involvement is particularly intriguing.

The UFC chief is partnered with Alalshikh through Zuffa Boxing and featured prominently in the announcement, with Netflix describing the event as a collaboration involving White and Alalshikh's The Ring. Hearn and Warren were absent.

Hearn had previously said White would not be involved in promoting the fight, while Warren says both fighters' contracts stipulated the same.

Yet Warren says White ultimately helped secure the Netflix deal but believes fans care little about the promotional politics.

"I don't know whether he will be front and centre or not," Warren said.

Wednesday's news conference in London may tell us more - not least how prominent White is and how he and Hearn share the stage after months of back-and-forth.

Ringwalk and what happens to the winner?

Even Cardiff comes with competing claims of credit.

Hearn had publicly pushed for the Principality Stadium in recent weeks, while Warren told BBC Sport Queensberry and Saudi events company Sela spent several months working "quietly" with the venue and local authorities.

The stadium's retractable roof makes it well suited to a December event and there is precedent for late night boxing.

Joe Calzaghe's victory over Mikkel Kessler there in 2007 took place under a closed roof, with the fight starting after 01:00 GMT to accommodate American television. Fury-Joshua is expected to follow a similar pattern.

The exact ringwalk time remains in the hands of Netflix, with Hearn saying his current understanding is around 01:00 or 01:30 GMT. Warren has ruled out anything as late as 04:00.

"If it went on in America you'd be watching it five o'clock in the morning," Warren said. "It's a compromise and it's an event."

There is no contractual rematch clause, according to Hearn. "We're coming in for the kind of victory that no-one will need to see the fight again," he said.

Warren believes the winner can continue towards further world-title opportunities. For the loser, he thinks the road may end in Cardiff.

Whatever the outcome, Fury-Joshua has long been defined by the reasons it did not happen.

But in just over eleven weeks there will be no more negotiations, competing claims or hypothetical outcomes - just Fury and Joshua, in the same ring at last.

articles.title: Fury and Joshua meet Dec. 11 in Cardiff after years of false starts
articles.summary: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have circled each other since 2015. On Dec. 11, at Principality Stadium in Cardiff, the false starts finally end.
articles.body:
Just weeks ago, this fight looked like it might slip away again. Tyson Fury, frustrated over where the bout would actually take place, threatened to walk from the negotiating table entirely and floated a third fight with Oleksandr Usyk instead. It was the kind of near-collapse that's defined this matchup for a decade.

Fury and Anthony Joshua have circled each other since 2015, an all-British heavyweight rivalry that's survived Fury's chaos years, Joshua's title runs and losses, and more than one round of collapsed talks in between. Both men have fought almost everyone else first. Wilder trilogies, Usyk rematches, tune-up wins over lesser names, all while the fight British boxing actually wanted sat unfinished.

Oct 9, 2021; Las Vegas, Nevada, USA; Deontay Wilder (red/black trunks) and Tyson Fury (black/gold trunks) box during their WBC/Lineal heavyweight championship boxing match at T-Mobile Arena. Mandatory Credit: Joe Camporeale-USA TODAY Sports

That ends Dec. 11. Fury and Joshua will meet at Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales, streaming live worldwide on Netflix. Turki Alalshikh, owner of Ring Magazine and chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority made it official Thursday, writing that "for 15 years no one has been able to make this fight" before confirming it was finally done.

Sam Navarro - IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Dec 19, 2025; Miami, Florida, UNITED STATES; Anthony Joshua hits Jake Paul during a heavyweight boxing bout at Kaseya Center. Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images

The promotional setup is worth untangling. This isn't a Zuffa Boxing card in the way Garcia-Benn was. Ring Magazine, which Alalshikh owns, is promoting the fight, with UFC and Zuffa Boxing president Dana White partnered alongside him. Netflix carries the broadcast. It's a three-way arrangement that's become increasingly familiar in boxing's biggest fights this year.

It also fits a pattern White has talked about openly. At the Garcia-Benn presser last month, he described Zuffa's long game as building fight cards stacked from top to bottom, the same way UFC does, so fans show up excited for the whole night rather than one marquee bout. Fury-Joshua doesn't carry Zuffa's name on it, but it lands squarely in the orbit White and Alalshikh have been building around Netflix all year.

It's also arriving into a heavyweight division that's anything but unified. Agit Kabayel is expected to lock in his first WBC title defense for November in Germany. Usyk, meanwhile, is eyeing Deontay Wilder for March 2027. Fury-Joshua carries no title implications at all, but it's arguably the biggest heavyweight fight on the calendar regardless of what any of the belts say.

And that's the point. No world championship is at stake Dec. 11, but few fights in the sport carry this much weight without one. Fury and Joshua are both former unified champions, both massive commercial draws, and both have spent the better part of a decade with this specific rivalry hanging over their careers. This was always going to be a legacy fight first.

Nov 21, 2025; Miami, Florida, UNITED STATES; Anthony Joshua speaks to reporters during a press conference announcing his heavyweight boxing match against Jake Paul at Kaseya Center. Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images

The location fight explains why it almost didn't happen. Joshua reportedly had UK soil written into his deal from the start, unwilling to budge on bringing the fight home. Fury preferred a bigger stage in the U.S. and pushed back hard enough that talks nearly fell apart again before Cardiff won out.

Feb 21, 2020; Las Vegas, Nevada, USA; Tyson Fury reacts after weighing in for his world heavyweight championship boxing match against Deontay Wilder (not pictured) at MGM Grand Garden Arena. Mandatory Credit: Joe Camporeale-USA TODAY Sports

Where it goes from here matters just as much as the fight itself. A Fury win keeps his name in the Usyk conversation, and the clock is a real factor there. Usyk has said he's eyeing retirement in the next couple of years, meaning a Fury-Usyk trilogy fight might not happen at all if Fury doesn't get through Joshua first.

A Joshua win reopens doors that looked closed a year ago. Either way, it's one more heavyweight domino falling into place in a division that's currently split across three different promotional worlds. For Fury and Joshua, though, Dec. 11 is something this fight hasn't had in over a decade: an actual date and location.

articles.title: How Eric Nicksick ended up cornering Sean Sharaf for shock knockout at UFC 331
articles.summary: Eric Nicksick only found out about cornering Sean Sharaf at UFC 331 hours before.
articles.body:
Eric Nicksick only found out about cornering Sean Sharaf at UFC 331 hours before.

Sharaf (5-2 MMA, 1-2 UFC) scored one of the biggest upsets in UFC history when he knocked out Gable Steveson (4-1 MMA, 1-1 UFC) this past Saturday at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

Sharaf sought help from Xtreme Couture head honcho Nicksick after an emergency ruled out UFC heavyweight Serghei Spivac from his corner. Nicksick was caught off guard when he was approached.

"I've known Sean for a while," Nicksick told MMA Junkie Radio. "He's been cross-training in and out of Xtreme. Sean Strickland and I cornered him for the Junior Tafa fight. That was on short notice. I believe he got that fight on like three or four days' notice. So we're very familiar with each other, but it was kind of crazy how everything went down. I was in the back and we're warming up Edmen Shahbazyan, and then a couple of UFC personnel came back there and they're like, 'Hey, what do you need for Sean's Sharaf's corner?' And I was like, 'What are you talking about? I don't even know what you're talking about.'

"I was like, '(Jason) Manly's in his corner. And they're like, 'No, he just wrote us and said that he needs you to hop in the corner.' I'm so confused. He's got my number. So I went and called (Sharaf) and then it went straight to voicemail or like a disconnected number. I'm like, this is weird, dude. I don't know what the hell's going on. And then I looked at those like unknowns in your text messages and he must have changed his number. So, I had like a text from him and it was like, 'Yo coach, if it's a problem, just say no, but I need you in my corner. Serghei Spivac, his wife (is) having the baby. So can you just hop in my corner for me?' I was like, 'Sure, brother. I'm there.'"

Nicksick recalls having a brief conversation with Sharaf regarding the matchup, but takes zero credit for his monumental moment.

"I talked with them a little bit in the PI a while back. He just kind of went over a few little things that he was asking about, like concept wise vs. Gable," Nicksick said. "We spent like 20 minutes together, so there was no game plan. There's a couple things that we went over, and then in the back, I watched a little bit of tape and literally the only thing I was talking to him about was when Gable goes southpaw. I was like, 'Hey, when he's southpaw, these are the things that I'm seeing,' and none of that even mattered.

"So we were just in there, and he was going over a couple things, and helped him with a couple routes and that was that, man. He did everything. His coach and camp, they all worked on everything that they did in preparation for him for that fight. They did an excellent job. I just had the best seat in the house. ... I was backseat to one of the best underdog moments of MMA history. It was pretty cool to be a part of."
authors: Farah Hannoun, George Garcia and Brian Garcia, MMA Junkie

articles.title: Fisher vs Pirotton: How far can the British heavyweight go?
articles.summary: British heavyweight Johnny Fisher - who returns to the Copper Box for his Zuffa Boxing debut on Saturday - reflects on defeat, fame and his rebuild.
articles.body:
When Johnny Fisher steps back inside the Copper Box Arena on Saturday night, the surroundings will feel familiar, even if much around his career has changed.

The east London venue was once something of a fortress for Fisher, where John Denver's 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' accompanied his ring walk and thousands of supporters reacted to every punch as his unbeaten record grew.

That changed last year when Dave Allen stopped him in the fifth round, handing the heavyweight his first professional defeat and leading critics to question his standing in the division.

Now the 27-year-old returns to headline against Belgium's Michael Pirotton in a 10-round contest which also marks his promotional debut for Dana White's Zuffa Boxing.

"Yeah, I had a loss, but one loss can't define your career," Fisher tells BBC Sport.

"There are many, many people before me who are much better than me who have lost and come back."

Fisher's rise has been far from conventional. With only a handful of amateur bouts and a background playing university rugby, he became a major domestic ticket-seller while still learning his trade.

Much of that appeal came alongside his father, 'Big John'. Their Chinese takeaway reviews, Essex humour and cries of "Bosh" found an audience beyond boxing and helped create the travelling support known as the Bosh Army.

Fisher won his first 13 professional fights, but his first meeting with Allen in December 2024 exposed vulnerabilities as he escaped with a controversial split-decision victory. Five months later, Allen stopped him in the fifth round, while his comeback against Ivan Balaz was also unconvincing despite a fourth-round stoppage win.

Those performances sharpened questions over Fisher's boxing credentials and exposed him to a harsher side of the attention that had accompanied his rise.

"Of course my fanbase is loyal to me," he says. "But when things are going well, people want to jump on the bandwagon and when it goes wrong there'll be people who are the first ones to say, 'we knew he'd never do it,' or 'he's no good.'"

There were also online jibes that Fisher was better suited to crossover boxing than the serious heavyweight scene, but he firmly rejects the suggestion his popularity makes him an influencer boxer.

"There are guys who have hardly any boxing experience whatsoever who have millions of followers on YouTube. You think of the Jake Pauls and the Tommy Furys, who aren't even at my level," he says.

"If people want to watch you and you've got a following - which I have through me and my dad - it's a magical thing. But it's not as if I'm in that influencer sphere. I'm a professional boxer first and foremost."

After five years with Eddie Hearn's Matchroom, Fisher signed with Zuffa Boxing in July, admitting the deal was simply too good to ignore.

"I got made a fantastic financial offer, which I would be lying if I said I could turn down," he says. "Our health isn't guaranteed in this sport, let alone our financials."

His first proper meeting with White came, suitably, over a Chinese meal with his father. "It was great to break bread - or prawn crackers - over a Chinese," Fisher adds.

There has been change in the gym too. Fisher left long-time trainer Mark Tibbs for Tony Sims and admits there had previously been an element of "winging it" in his preparation.

This camp, he says, has included around 160 rounds of sparring, altitude work and 6am hill sprints.

For all the change, though, Fisher's own assessment of his level remains relatively modest. "I'm not Usyk, I'm no AJ, I'm not Fury," he says. "I'm not these top guys at the top of the division."

He mentions Frazer Clarke and Solomon Dacres as possible domestic opponents and says fighting for the British title within 12 to 18 months would be "amazing".

Current champion Richard Riakporhe has already welcomed the prospect of facing him if Fisher beats Pirotton, although the former cruiserweight world-title challenger would represent a considerable step up.

"All I've got to do is win my next fight," Fisher adds. "That's the only thing that matters, and then the picture becomes clearer. My aspiration is always to have a good time and have a good old swing at it."
